newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia 1997/98 winter crop seen falling.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia 1997/98 winter crop seen falling.

text.p: Total plantings of Australian winter crops in 1997/98 (July-June) are forecast to decline by around 2.5 percent, the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE) said on Tuesday.

The decline reflects expectations of lower prices versus 1996/97, some limited rebuilding in sheep numbers and a return to more normal crop rotation patterns after the disruption of an extended drought in the states of Queensland and New south Wales, ABARE said in its latest Australian Crop Report.
"Currently, soil conditions are good in most winter cropping regions, with some relatively small areas being excessively wet," ABARE said.
Soil conditions are enabling growers to complete early land preparation meaning only modest rains are needed to allow winter crop planting intentions in 1997/98 to be realised, it said.
Forecast gross margins for crops and crop rotational requirements tend to favour increased production of pulses and oilseeds, particularly canola, at the expense of wheat and barley, ABARE said.
Wheat plantings are forecast to decline by 500,000 hectares in 1997/98, ABARE said.
Plantings of canola are expected to increase by 51 percent in 1997/98 as producers continue to respond to favourable prices and utilise new varieties, it said.
This is particularly the case in Western Australia, where the seed orders suggest that plantings could increase to over 200,000 hectares in 1997/98 from 90,000 in 1996/97, ABARE said.
"However, for all states to achieve the expansion that seed orders suggest, early planting rains are critical," ABARE said.
Assuming average yields, Australia's canola production is forecast to increase to around 820,000 tonnes in 1997/98, from 616,000 in 1996/97, ABARE said.
ABARE is the Australian government's commodities forecasting agency.
